title: When sakhis differ
hookLine: traditions sometimes tell the same story in different places; the lesson usually stays the same

lines: HE GAVE THE COAT EITHER WAY.
THE JANAMSAKHIS HAVE DINNERS LIKE THAT.
cards: At a family dinner, two cousins start telling the same story about their grandfather. One says it happened at the train station. The other says no, it was the market, and it was raining.
They argue about the rain for five minutes. Then someone at the end of the table says: does it matter? He gave the man his coat either way.
Everyone goes quiet, because that was the whole point of the story. The janamsakhis have dinners like that too.

teach.b: This block began with the janamsakhis and their families: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's reflective one, the illustrated pages. They don't always agree.
A sakhi set in one town in one collection may turn up somewhere else in another; a detail added in one is missing in the next.

You've met it already: tellings place Mardana's death in different places, and differ on what the king did with Bhumia. How do you hold that? Go back to what a sakhi is: truth carried in the shape of a story.
A news report lives or dies by where and when.

teach.h: A SAKHI LIVES BY WHAT IT TEACHES.
teach.b: A sakhi lives by what it teaches.
So watch what stays put when the details move. Mardana refuses a tomb, wherever he dies. Bhumia's three promises hold, whatever the king decides.
Historians compare tellings to learn which material looks older and how stories traveled; that work isn't an attack on the sakhis, it's a kind of care for them.
And a teller who says, in some tellings it was here, in others there, is being honest.
Sikh tradition gives its highest authority to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to any janamsakhi, so the stories can differ without the ground moving.

how: Sikh teachers telling a sakhi may note that tellings differ, and the Guru Granth Sahib, not any janamsakhi, is treated as the Guru and final authority.

practice: Bring to mind a story you know two ways, a family story, a news story, or a sakhi from this month, and notice where the tellings part. Don't decide which is right; let both stand side by side, and ask what they share.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.
